strengths: Novel and well-motivated insight: identifying that diffusion self-attention transiently encodes instance-level boundaries (Instance Emergence Point) is an interesting finding that is clearly supported by qualitative and quantitative evidence (Tab. 5, Fig. 8), distinguishing TRACE from both DINO-based UIS methods and prior diffusion segmentation work (DiffCut/DiffSeg) that operate at semantic timesteps.

Well-designed framework: IEP + ABDiv + one-step self-distillation form a coherent pipeline, and the distillation cleverly converts a slow per-image forward-process procedure (3s/image) into a single 45ms pass (81x speedup) while improving edge connectivity.

Strong empirical results across settings: consistent gains over UIS baselines on COCO/VOC (+3.6 to +5.3 AP), a 2.3x average improvement over seven benchmarks in Appendix E, and a headline result where tag-only supervision surpasses point-supervised panoptic baselines on VOC and COCO.

Thorough ablations and analysis: component ablation (Tab. 3), KL vs. JSD/MSE/MAE for IEP and ABDiv (Tab. 4), IEP stride/latency trade-off and timestep distribution (Fig. 7), reconstruction-loss ablation, and a convincing comparison against conventional edge detectors (Canny/HED/PiDiNet/DiffusionEdge) showing the instance-vs-texture boundary distinction.
Reproducibility: complete codebase in supplementary material, algorithmic pseudocode for all modules, implementation details, and computational overhead reporting (Tab. 6).
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains low in the core unsupervised setting (e.g., ~8-9 AP on COCO vs. ~60 PQ for fully supervised), so the practical significance of 'practical and scalable alternative to manual annotation' is somewhat overstated; TRACE is currently best viewed as a refinement signal for existing pipelines rather than a standalone solution.

Potential train/test contamination and fairness concerns: the diffusion backbone (SD3.5-L, 8.1B params) is pretrained on internet-scale captioned data and then LoRA fine-tuned on ImageNet before being applied to COCO/VOC/LVIS/KITTI/Objects365/SA-1B, while baselines use much smaller DINO backbones; the paper does not discuss whether the generative prior has effectively 'seen' benchmark images, which weakens the 'annotation-free' framing.

Some inconsistency and mild overclaiming: the abstract claims +5.1 AP while the contributions list +4.4 AP; the +16.5 PQ (stuff) claim for SAM seeds is cherry-picked; the headline VOC result (69.8 PQ) uses Swin-L which requires a separate comparison row against EPLD Swin-L (68.5), a modest +1.3 gain.

Key design choices are empirically justified but weakly grounded theoretically: why KL divergence between neighboring pixel attention distributions specifically peaks on instance boundaries, and why a global mean+-sigma threshold is robust across diverse images, are asserted rather than analyzed; the ternary supervision thresholding introduces hyperparameters not ablated.

Heavy computational requirements (10 days of A100 training, 32GB VRAM for the SD3.5-L variant) somewhat undercut the efficiency narrative, and the per-image IEP search (~3s) is required whenever re-training for a new domain, limiting scalability claims.

Writing quality is mixed: several typos/grammatical issues (e.g., 'or boxes, or masks', missing closing parenthesis in Sec. 5), and Sec. 3.5's BGP description is thin in the main paper, relying on Appendix D.6.

strengths: The core observation that diffusion self-attention briefly encodes instance-level structure (Instance Emergence Point) is interesting and the analysis of timestep distributions across backbones (Fig. 7b, Tab. 5) is a useful empirical contribution.

The paper is broad in scope: it touches unsupervised instance segmentation, tag-supervised panoptic segmentation, and SAM-based pipelines, with consistent reported gains across many benchmarks (COCO, VOC, LVIS, KITTI, Objects365, SA-1B).

The component ablation (Tab. 3), metric ablation (Tab. 4), stride analysis (Fig. 7a), and edge-detector comparison (Fig. 10) are reasonably thorough, and the paper includes detailed algorithms and a codebase for reproducibility.
The one-step distillation to remove per-image inversion is a sensible engineering solution that reduces inference latency substantially relative to the naive teacher pipeline.
weaknesses: Fragile baseline story and confounded gains: all headline numbers come from plugging TRACE+BGP into very weak UIS baselines (MaskCut, ProMerge, AP around 3-5). It is unclear how much of the improvement comes from the diffusion edges versus the Boundary-Guided Propagation refinement itself — BGP is not independently ablated against edges from a random/confident detector, so the claimed attribution to 'secretly an instance edge detector' is not cleanly supported.

Low absolute performance and questionable significance: even with TRACE, AP on COCO remains ~8-15 and far below trivially supervised or even open-vocabulary alternatives. Claiming to 'surpass point-supervised panoptic models' while using a far stronger backbone (SD3.5-L, 8.1B params) and ImageNet-scale unsupervised fine-tuning is not an apples-to-apples supervision comparison; compute and data budgets are not equalized across the compared methods.

Heavy computational and supervision footprint: TRACE fine-tunes a large diffusion backbone (10 days on an A100, 32GB VRAM) on each target dataset family, whereas baselines like MaskCut/ProMerge are training-free or use much lighter models. The '81x faster' claim only applies relative to the paper's own per-image IEP+ABDiv teacher, not to any competing method.

Unclear novelty: extracting segmentation-relevant structure from diffusion attention at specific timesteps is well-trodden (DiffCut, DiffSeg, ConceptAttention). The contribution largely reduces to choosing a KL-based timestep and a neighbor-divergence edge heuristic, followed by standard self-distillation and existing random-walk propagation (Ahn et al.), which limits the conceptual advance.

Equation and notation issues: Eq. 1 defines IEP over consecutive inversion timesteps with an unclear argmax over discrete steps; the ABDiv ternary thresholding with global mean +/- std is brittle and image-content dependent, and the paper provides little analysis of failure modes (e.g., scenes with objects sharing appearance, heavy overlap, or stuff regions that could be falsely separated into instances).

Quantitative support for several bold claims is thin: the '+5.1 AP' and '+1.7 PQ' headline numbers do not consistently match the tables (e.g., Tab. 1 shows up to +5.3 on some settings but +4.4 elsewhere), and comparisons to open-vocabulary detectors via SAM seeding (Fig. 9) mix supervision types without controlled setups.

Training the edge decoder requires pseudo-edge labels generated by the full IEP+ABDiv teacher, which itself inherits the diffusion model's biases (e.g., training-data object priors), yet the paper markets the method as 'unbiased' versus human annotation (Fig. 3) without evidence for that claim.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated insight: the paper shows that text-to-image diffusion self-attention transiently encodes instance-level boundaries during denoising (the Instance Emergence Point), and that this signal can be extracted non-parametrically (ABDiv) and distilled into a one-step decoder. This is a fresh angle compared to prior diffusion-segmentation works (DiffCut, DiffSeg) that operate at later, semantic timesteps.

Strong and broad empirical evidence: consistent gains across multiple UIS baselines (MaskCut, ProMerge, CutLER, ProMerge+) and seven benchmarks (VOC, COCO 2014/2017, LVIS, KITTI, Objects365, SA-1B), plus the notable result that tag-supervised panoptic segmentation with TRACE surpasses point-supervised baselines without any instance labels.

Thorough ablation and analysis: component ablation (Tab. 3), KL vs. alternative divergences for both IEP and ABDiv (Tab. 4), IEP stride accuracy-latency trade-off and timestep distribution across five backbones (Fig. 7), diffusion vs. non-diffusion backbones including large MLLMs (Tab. 5), and comparison against conventional edge detectors (Fig. 10) all support the design choices.

Practical considerations are addressed: the one-step distillation removes per-image IEP/ABDiv cost (81x faster at inference), computational overhead is reported (Tab. 6), and a complete codebase is provided in supplementary material with a reproducibility statement.
Fair baseline treatment: authors reproduce point-supervised and UIS baselines with public code where applicable and clearly mark reproduced vs. reported numbers.
weaknesses: Absolute UIS performance remains low (APmk of ~8-15 even with TRACE), so the reported gains, while consistent, are from a very low base; the practical significance of the edge prior in absolute terms could be better contextualized.

Inconsistency in headline claims: the abstract reports +5.1 AP improvement for unsupervised instance segmentation while the contribution list states +4.4 AP; similarly '81x faster' applies only to the distilled decoder, not the full method. These should be reconciled.

Potential confound of capacity: TRACE relies on a very large backbone (SD3.5-L, 8.1B params) with LoRA fine-tuning, whereas UIS baselines use DINO-based backbones (~0.3-1.1B). Although Tab. 5 controls within diffusion backbones, a cleaner capacity-matched comparison (e.g., a large non-diffusion model with equivalent fine-tuning) would strengthen the claim that the gain is from the instance-emergent attention signal rather than scale.

The generalization setup raises questions: for cross-dataset UIS, the diffusion model and edge generator are fine-tuned on ImageNet, and downstream UIS/WSS models still leverage their own pretrained (possibly noisy-label-trained) backbones; the boundary between 'annotation-free' and 'distilled supervision from pretrained models' deserves more explicit discussion.

The claim that tag supervision 'first surpasses point-supervised panoptic baselines' holds most convincingly on VOC with Swin-L; on COCO the gap over point-supervised EPLD (43.1 vs 41.0 PQ) is smaller and could be affected by evaluation subset choices.

Some methodological details are under-specified or rely on heuristics (e.g., the mu +/- sigma ternary thresholding of ABDiv, the fixed inversion stride of 100, tau_BGP = 0.5), and the paper would benefit from sensitivity analysis on the thresholding parameters; the BGP random-walk step is largely borrowed from prior work (Ahn et al., 2018/2019) and is described only at a high level.
Training overhead is non-trivial (8-10 days on an A100 for the distillation stage), which somewhat tempers the scalability narrative, and no error bars or multiple-seed results are reported.

strengths: Compelling and clearly articulated core insight: self-attention maps of text-to-image diffusion models transiently encode instance-level boundaries at specific denoising timesteps, which the authors exploit via two simple, principled components (IEP via KL peak, ABDiv via criss-cross neighbor divergence).

Strong empirical results across many settings: consistent AP gains (+3.6 to +5.3) over unsupervised instance segmentation baselines on VOC/COCO and seven additional benchmarks, and tag-supervised panoptic segmentation that surpasses point-supervised methods (+1.7 to +7.1 PQ), a meaningful threshold crossing for the field.

Thorough component ablations (Tab. 3, 4, 9, 10) that isolate the contribution of each stage; the ablation showing that ABDiv at a purely semantic timestep yields almost no gain is a convincing validation of the central claim.

A nice cross-backbone comparison (Tab. 5, Fig. 8) demonstrating the effect is specific to diffusion/flow models, including beating a 72B non-diffusion model with a 0.6B diffusion model; this strengthens the 'diffusion prior' claim beyond anecdote.

One-step self-distillation is practically important: removing per-image IEP/ABDiv (3682ms to 45ms, 81x faster) makes the approach deployable, and the decoder capacity ablation shows gains come from the edge cues rather than model capacity.

Theoretical appendix (D) provides an information-theoretic justification (inter-step KL ~ Fisher information at peak), explaining why different f-divergences locate the same IEP — supported empirically in Tab. 11.
Honest and detailed limitations section (tiny objects in satellite imagery, out-of-distribution medical images) with quantitative degradation results, which is unusual and commendable.
Comprehensive appendix: method details, algorithms, reproduction details, new instance-edge benchmark derived from COCO panoptic masks, extensive qualitative figures.
weaknesses: Absolute performance in unsupervised instance segmentation remains low (AP of ~8-15), so the practical significance of the UIS gains, while relatively large, should be tempered; the headline framing could be read as stronger than the raw numbers.

The method leans on very large text-to-image backbones (SD3.5-L, 8.1B params; FLUX 12B), and the 10-day training cost and 32GB VRAM are nontrivial; a cost/benefit discussion relative to lighter alternatives (e.g., DINO-based methods) could be expanded.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior diffusion-attention segmentation work (DiffCut, DiffSeg, EmerDiff); the differentiator (timestep selection + boundary divergence rather than clustering at fixed timesteps) is convincing but the overall pipeline (attention -> edges -> pseudo-labels -> distill) follows a familiar recipe.
The 81x speedup claim is relative to the authors' own non-distilled variant, not to competing pipelines; some readers may find the framing slightly overstated.

Some baselines are reproduced with asterisks and hyperparameter-sensitive methods (MaskCut) are re-run by the authors; while the protocol appears careful, independent verification of gains against other recent methods (e.g., UnSAM variants, CutS3D on all datasets) is limited in places.
Several figures (e.g., Fig. 1, 9, 10) are dense and hard to parse; figure clarity would benefit from simplification.

The distillation is trained on ImageNet for cross-dataset transfer, which introduces a dataset mismatch (natural-image T2I model fine-tuned on ImageNet) that is not fully analyzed with respect to potential shortcut or bias effects.

strengths: The core observation (self-attention in diffusion models transiently encodes instance-level structure at a specific denoising step) is interesting and well-motivated with clear qualitative evidence (Figs. 1, 8).

The paper is unusually comprehensive in evaluation: 7 benchmarks for UIS, 2 for weakly-supervised panoptic segmentation, 10 backbones, multiple metric ablations (Tab. 4/11), decoder-capacity ablation (Tab. 9), pseudo-labeling ablation (Tab. 10), and an information-theoretic justification of the KL/IEP choice (Appendix D).
The one-step self-distillation design is practical, and the limitations section is refreshingly honest, with quantitative failure cases on satellite and medical imagery rather than hiding them.
Results are consistent across many datasets and settings (Tab. 12 shows broad transfer), suggesting the phenomenon is real rather than dataset-specific.
weaknesses: Absolute performance is low, and the headline gains are relative to very weak baselines. TRACE achieves only 7.5-8.2 AP on COCO 2017/2014 in training-free UIS and 12.8-13.3 AP when fine-tuned, versus ~52 PQ for fully supervised Mask2Former. A +5.1 AP improvement on a baseline at ~3 AP is not a competitive instance segmentation method; the practical significance of the results is overstated by the abstract's framing.

Comparison fairness is questionable. TRACE relies on an 8.1B-parameter diffusion model (SD3.5-L, pretrained on massive image-caption data and additionally fine-tuned 10 days on ImageNet) while UIS baselines use DINO ViT-B features. Table 5 presents diffusion backbones with IEP+ABDiv but non-diffusion backbones with ABDiv only, so the headline claim that 'diffusion models are secretly instance edge detectors' is partially confounded: the IEP mechanism (the largest source of gain in Tab. 3, 3.2 to 4.8) is only applicable to the diffusion branch by construction.

The edge-quality benchmark (Tab. 6, ODS 0.889) is constructed directly from COCO panoptic masks, and TRACE's edges are pseudo-supervised in a pipeline whose final goal is panoptic-mask refinement; the extremely large margin over DiffusionEdge may partly reflect this alignment/circularity rather than a fundamentally better edge detector, and competing detectors trained on BSDS contours are at an inherent objective disadvantage.

Computational cost is substantial and unevenly disclosed: 10 days of A100 training, 32 GB VRAM, ~3 s per image for IEP search during pseudo-label generation, versus lightweight DINO-based baselines requiring no training. The '81x faster' claim compares only against the paper's own non-distilled variant, not against baselines.

Novelty is moderate: extracting semantic structure from diffusion self-attention is well explored (DiffCut, DiffSeg, EmerDiff, ConceptAttention), and the technical contribution reduces to timestep selection via temporal KL divergence plus a neighborhood-divergence edge score and standard distillation/propagation machinery.

Some reproduced baselines (marked with *) show numbers notably below or divergent from original publications, and given the weak absolute regime, small reproduction differences could materially affect the reported gains.

The weakly-supervised panoptic comparison (Tab. 2) conflates supervision types: DHR+TRACE (tags only) beats point-supervised methods, but DHR alone gains 11.7 to 18.3 PQ on COCO from the WSS baseline change alone, so the attribution of the improvement to TRACE's edges versus the stronger semantic model needs more careful decomposition.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated core observation: diffusion self-attention transiently reveals instance-level structure at a specific denoising timestep, and this is systematically validated against non-diffusion backbones (Table 5, Fig. 8), supporting the central claim that instance boundary priors are intrinsic to generative diffusion models.

Technically clean pipeline: Instance Emergence Point (IEP) and Attention Boundary Divergence (ABDiv) are simple, non-parametric, and well-justified; the one-step self-distillation elegantly removes the expensive per-image IEP/ABDiv computation at inference (3682ms -> 45ms, ~81x speedup) while strengthening edge connectivity.

Comprehensive and convincing evaluation: consistent gains across unsupervised instance segmentation (+4.4 to +5.3 AP on COCO), weakly-supervised panoptic segmentation (surpassing point-supervised baselines with only image-level tags, e.g., 69.8 PQ on VOC), and open-vocabulary segmentation, spanning 11 datasets and 10 backbones.

Thorough ablations: component ablation (Tab. 3), IEP metric comparison including entropy/Wasserstein/JSD (Tab. 4, 11), decoder capacity (Tab. 9), pseudo-labeling scheme (Tab. 10), and distributional consistency of t* across models/datasets/classes (Fig. 14).

A theoretically grounded information-theoretic analysis in Appendix D connecting the IEP KL peak to maximal Fisher information, and showing all f-divergences share the same quadratic form, which explains metric choice.

Honest and detailed limitations section: quantified failure on satellite imagery (tiny instances) and medical imaging (OOD), with qualitative failure cases; theoretical work is clearly separated from empirical claims. Reproducibility details and protocols are provided.
weaknesses: Absolute performance of unsupervised instance segmentation remains low (e.g., 8-15 APmk on COCO/VOC even with TRACE), so the practical value of the UIS results is somewhat limited even though relative gains are large.

Training cost is substantial: 8-10 days on a single A100 with 20-32GB VRAM to fine-tune large diffusion backbones (SDXL, SD3.5-L, 8.1B params), which limits accessibility and reproducibility for groups without large GPUs; no results with a smaller distilled backbone as the deployed student are reported.

The instance-edge benchmark (Table 6) is self-constructed from COCO panoptic masks; while reasonable, edge-quality conclusions rely on this new benchmark and the massive ODS gap over DiffusionEdge (0.889 vs 0.428) reflects an objective mismatch rather than a head-to-head edge-detection comparison on equal footing.

Method inherits strong dependency on the specific generative prior of text-to-image diffusion models; results degrade with model size and fail entirely out-of-domain (satellite, medical), meaning the 'annotation-free' benefit does not transfer to domains where dense annotation is most costly.

Some presentation issues: occasional inconsistencies in reported gains (abstract says +5.1 AP, contributions say +4.4 AP), heavy reliance on reproduced baseline numbers, and the BGP merging threshold tau_BGP=0.5 is only validated on VOC, leaving its robustness on COCO/other benchmarks less clear.

The distillation uses ImageNet as the training set while evaluation is on COCO/VOC/LVIS etc.; although aligned with UIS protocol, the effect of training-set choice and potential leakage of natural-image statistics into 'unsupervised' claims could be analyzed more explicitly.
